nameStory: Canada St. John's wort gets its name from its Canadian origins and its membership in the St. John's wort family, plants traditionally associated with St. John the Baptist's feast day in late June. The 'lesser' part of its alternate name reflects its smaller, more delicate stature compared to its robust European cousin, Common St. John's wort.
description: Canada St. John's wort is a delicate, native wildflower that stands just 1-2 feet tall with a slender, branching stem. This annual or short-lived perennial produces small, bright yellow flowers with five petals that seem to glow in dappled sunlight. Its narrow, oval leaves grow opposite each other along the stem, and the whole plant has a wispy, almost fragile appearance compared to other St. John's worts. You'll often find it growing in small colonies in wet, sandy areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers about 1/4 inch across with 5 petals and numerous stamens creating a fuzzy center. Flowers feel papery-thin and are arranged in loose, open clusters at the stem tips.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. Hold a leaf up to the light and you may see tiny translucent dots scattered throughout - these are oil glands that feel slightly sticky when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, delicate plant 1-2 feet tall with thin, wiry stems that branch near the top. The whole plant has an airy, almost wispy quality and may lean or bend easily in the breeze.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, reddish-brown seed capsules that split into three parts when ripe, releasing tiny dark seeds. The capsules make a subtle rattling sound when shaken in late summer.

habitat: Look for Canada St. John's wort in wet, sandy or peaty soils along pond edges, in wet meadows, and boggy areas throughout New England. It thrives in acidic conditions and partial shade, often growing alongside sedges, wild cranberry, and other bog plants. This moisture-loving native prefers areas that stay damp most of the year but aren't permanently flooded.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of opposite leaves in late spring. Early growth is subtle and the plant may be overlooked among other emerging wetland vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers appear from July through August, making this the best time for identification. The delicate blooms are most noticeable in morning light when they seem to glow against the green foliage.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules ripen to reddish-brown, eventually splitting open. Leaves may turn yellowish before the annual plants die back completely.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving no above-ground trace. Only the seeds remain dormant in the soil until the next growing season.

funFact: Despite being called 'Canadian,' this little wildflower has somehow managed to hitchhike all the way to Ireland and the Netherlands, probably traveling as seeds stuck to migrating birds or hidden in soil on ships - making it one of the few North American plants to successfully colonize Europe rather than the other way around!
confusionNotes: Canada St. John's wort is easily confused with Dwarf St. John's wort, but Canada's flowers are larger and its leaves are more oval-shaped rather than narrow and linear. Remember: Canada = 'Chubby' leaves and flowers, while Dwarf has 'Dinky' narrow everything.
contextualKnowledge: Don't expect the same herbal properties from this delicate native that you might find in Common St. John's wort - Canada St. John's wort is much milder and wasn't traditionally used medicinally by Indigenous peoples the way some of its relatives were.
compareHints: Among New England's St. John's worts, Canada St. John's wort is one of the most delicate and water-loving species. While Common St. John's wort grows tall and robust in dry fields, and Spotted St. John's wort has distinctive black-dotted petals, Canada St. John's wort stays small and seeks out wet, boggy places. Its flowers are also notably smaller and more delicate than most of its relatives.
